For populations of the Arno goby Padogobius nigricans inhabiting the fluvial systems of central Italy, egg development proceeds slowly under the cool groundwater influence of many of these streams. The yolky, adhesive eggs are deposited beneath stones by a single gravid female and are guarded by the male until the prolarvae emerge. At a stable water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the incubation period from oviposition to chorion rupture lasts approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days], a duration that places this species among the more slowly developing Gobiidae of temperate Europe. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00016 grams [Wwb = 0.00016 grams] based on the dimensions of the fertilised ovum. This minute starting mass, coupled with a limited yolk reserve, means that the lecithotrophic phase is brief, and exogenous feeding must commence within a few days of eclosion if starvation is to be avoided, a pattern common among freshwater benthic gobies with small clutch components.

Sexual maturation in male and female Arno gobies follows a clear size-based trajectory, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm]. At this point, body mass has increased substantially from the hatchling stage, with the corresponding wet weight at puberty calculated at 2.25 grams [Wwp = 2.25 grams] from the length-weight relationship established for this species. The onset of gonadal activity at this size is consistent with observations from other Padogobius species, where a minimum threshold length is required before the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is activated. Field surveys across the Tiber and Arno catchments indicate that most males establish nesting territories and display reproductive coloration only after surpassing this 6 cm threshold, and females sampled below this length invariably possess undifferentiated, translucent gonads. This evidence underscores the importance of using a size-based rather than a strictly age-based metric for defining the onset of reproductive capability in this sedentary, river-dwelling fish.

Female Arno gobies continue to grow after sexual maturation, eventually reaching an ultimate total length of 12.5 cm [Li = 12.5 cm]. The corresponding asymptotic wet weight for females at this maximum size has been estimated at 20.5 grams [Wwi = 20.5 grams], derived from a length-weight power function fitted to a large sample of individuals from the species’ core range. This adult body mass is moderate compared to other freshwater gobiids, reflecting the relatively low productivity of the oligotrophic streams that P. nigricans typically inhabits. Mature females at this size are capable of producing multiple clutches per breeding season, and the reproductive investment is considerable relative to body mass. The species’ iteroparous life history, combined with a protracted spawning period that extends from late spring through early summer, allows for the gradual replenishment of population numbers despite the constraints imposed by a restricted benthic habitat and competition for nesting sites with the invasive congener Padogobius bonelli outside the Arno goby’s native range.

At a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the average gonadosomatic index (GSI) recorded during the peak of the spawning season is 9% [GSI = 9%]. Field observations confirm that gravid females collected during June at this temperature exhibit distinct abdominal distension, and histological examination of their ovaries reveals a high proportion of yolked, tertiary oocytes. The physiological decision to allocate such a substantial fraction of somatic resources to egg production likely reflects the selective pressure to maximise fecundity in an environment where larval survival is highly unpredictable and nest success is low.

Longevity records derived from mark-recapture studies of Arno goby populations indicate a maximum lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] under prevailing conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], which corresponds to five complete annual cycles. This moderately short lifespan is characteristic of a small-bodied, fast-living freshwater fish that faces high predation pressure from avian piscivores and larger European eels. Most individuals die after one or two breeding seasons, with very few surviving to the oldest age classes; the senescence observed in the final year is marked by a notable loss of body condition, diminished territorial behaviour, and a reduced spawning output. The trade-off between early, repeated reproduction and somatic maintenance is evident in this species, as the energetic demands of guarding nests, courting females, and fending off rivals throughout the extended breeding season exact a cumulative toll that ultimately limits the duration of the post-pubertal adult stage. Maximum recorded longevity in a closely related congener is similar.
